title: Exploring Antitrust and Platform Power in Generative AI
venue: 1st Workshop on Generative AI and Law, co-located with the International Conference on Machine Learning
extended_summary:
This paper examines antitrust and platform power in the generative AI ecosystem. Rather than studying an educational intervention or learner outcomes, it asks how market dominance is structured across the generative AI technology stack and whether current legal frameworks are adequate to address concentration of power among major technology firms.

The authors analyze the inputs and dependencies that shape success in generative AI, including access to large-scale data, top engineering talent, substantial capital, proprietary infrastructure, and the ability to fund and influence research. They discuss examples such as OpenAI/Microsoft, Google, Amazon, GitHub Copilot, and BloombergGPT to illustrate how incumbent firms may leverage existing advantages across adjacent markets.

The paper’s main conclusion is that generative AI is currently highly concentrated and vertically integrated, making it difficult for new entrants to compete. The authors argue that antitrust law and emerging AI regulation may unintentionally reinforce existing market power rather than reduce it, and they call for more substantial quantitative analysis of relevant AI markets in future work. The paper is a legal/technical position piece with no empirical study of participants or educational settings.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/legal analysis of antitrust and platform power in generative AI, not an empirical education study. It does not evaluate a learning intervention, report a study design, or present student outcome data.
impact_tier_rationale: No educational intervention or learner outcome is assessed, so there is no measurable K-12 impact to assign.
